nameStory: The Crystal Brain Fungus gets its memorable name from its translucent, watery-white appearance that resembles brain tissue, complete with the folded and convoluted surface. The 'crystal' part comes from tiny white mineral inclusions that sparkle like little crystals embedded throughout the gelatinous flesh, visible even to the naked eye.
description: Crystal Brain Fungus is a bizarre, jelly-like fungus that looks like a translucent white brain sitting on a log. These gelatinous blobs have a pustular or lobed surface with distinctive white mineral specks scattered throughout their watery flesh. They typically grow as small, rounded masses ranging from marble-sized to golf ball-sized, though they can sometimes form larger colonies that flow together along dead branches.

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Completely gelatinous and jelly-like to the touch, with a firm but bouncy consistency that springs back when poked

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Translucent watery white throughout, sometimes with a slight yellowish tinge, allowing you to see through parts of the fungus

idTips.label: Surface Features
idTips.description: Brain-like surface with pustules, bumps, and folded lobes, embedded with tiny white crystalline specks visible to the naked eye

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing directly on dead branches or logs of broadleaf trees, never on conifers or soil

idTips.label: Form
idTips.description: Grows as rounded, blob-like masses that can merge together to form larger flowing colonies along the wood surface

habitat: Look for Crystal Brain Fungus on dead branches and fallen logs of broadleaf trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. It particularly favors maple, oak, birch, and beech wood, growing directly from the bark surface of both attached dead branches and fallen timber. You'll find it in moist woodland areas where decomposing hardwood is plentiful, from lowland forests to mid-elevation slopes.

seasonality.spring: Begins appearing as temperatures warm and spring rains provide consistent moisture. Fresh specimens are most translucent and jelly-like during wet spring weather.
seasonality.summer: Continues fruiting during humid periods and after summer rainstorms. May temporarily shrivel during dry spells but revives with moisture.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for Crystal Brain Fungus, with abundant fruiting bodies appearing on newly fallen branches and logs. Cool, wet autumn weather provides ideal conditions.
seasonality.winter: Can persist through mild winter periods, though growth slows significantly. Existing specimens may freeze and thaw repeatedly, becoming less gelatinous.

funFact: Crystal Brain Fungus acts like a natural sponge - it can shrink down to a hard, dark crust during dry periods, then magically puff back up to its full jelly-like glory within hours of getting wet, making it nearly immortal as long as moisture eventually returns!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other jelly fungi like Witch's Butter, but Crystal Brain is the only translucent white jelly fungus with visible white mineral inclusions. Remember: if it's brain-shaped, translucent white, and has sparkly white specks throughout, you've found Crystal Brain.
contextualKnowledge: In North America, this fungus is sometimes called 'granular jelly roll,' though scientists aren't entirely sure if our North American specimens are the same species as the European Crystal Brain Fungus. The jury is still out on whether we're looking at identical twins or close cousins separated by an ocean.
compareHints: Crystal Brain Fungus is the only Myxarium species reliably found in New England. It differs from other jelly fungi in the region by its unique combination of brain-like surface texture, translucent white color, and distinctive white mineral inclusions that sparkle throughout the gelatinous flesh. Unlike Witch's Butter which is bright yellow-orange, or other clear jelly fungi that lack the mineral specks, Crystal Brain has a very distinctive appearance once you know what to look for.
